objective: By the end of the lesson, learners will have practised and developed the sub-skills of reading for gist and detailed comprehension in the context of an introduction to Every Day by David Levithan.
materials:
- Every Day by David Levithan (Chapter 1)
- YouTube trailer: Every Day - Official Trailer (2018) — https://youtu.be/dRvKm__GrqU
- Chapter 1 handout (includes reflection questions)

stages.stage_aim: To activate learners' interest in the novel and build anticipation.
stages.procedure:
- Show the Every Day trailer (~2 min).
- Elicit initial reactions: 'What do you think this story is about?'
- Pair discussion: 'What would it be like to wake up in a different body every day?'
- Brief class feedback (2 min).
- Bridge to the novel: 'Every Day is about a person named A who wakes up in a different body each morning. Today we will read Chapter 1 together.'

stages.stage_aim: To give learners context about the author and the novel's significance.
stages.procedure:
- Present David Levithan facts: born 1972, editor at Scholastic, wrote Every Day in his spare time, published 2012, adapted into a film in 2018.
- Key fact: Every Day has been translated into over 30 languages and won multiple YA awards.
- Show composite cast image from the film adaptation.
- Pre-teach selected vocabulary: inhabit, drifter, ephemeral, profound, transparent (brief board presentation with context from the chapter).

stages.stage: Setting the Purpose — Why Read Aloud?
stages.stage_aim: To establish the rationale for the reading circle format.
stages.procedure:
- Elicit: 'Why do we read out loud together in a reading circle?'
- Highlight benefits: improves fluency, builds vocabulary through context, creates a shared experience, helps hear the natural rhythm of English.
- Explain the lesson format: 20 min guided read-aloud, followed by private reading with reflection questions.

stages.stage_aim: To guide learners through the opening of the novel and develop reading fluency.
stages.procedure:
- Teacher and students take turns reading paragraphs aloud — each student reads 1-2 paragraphs then passes.
- Pause after the first page: 'What is unusual about the narrator?' (A wakes up in a different body each day)
- Pause after the beach scene (around 'I take her hand'): 'Why is A breaking the rules? What does Rhiannon represent for A?'
- As A's voice emerges, note key character traits: self-aware, lonely, curious, compassionate.
- Draw attention to the central question: Can A ever truly connect with someone?

stages.stage_aim: To give learners time to absorb the text individually and respond personally.
stages.procedure:
- Students re-read the chapter silently or continue from where the read-aloud stopped.
- Hand out reflection questions.
- Students write answers for themselves — this is not assessed, just a way to think about the text.
- If time permits, invite 1-2 students to share one thing they wrote with the class.

reflection_questions: 1. A says being a drifter is "lonely" but also "remarkably freeing." Which parts of A's life sound hard? Which parts sound good?
2. A decides to break the rules to spend the day with Rhiannon. Do you think it was worth it? What would you have done?
